traveler: Amir Khusrow Dehlavi (Abu'l Hasan Yamin ud-Din Khusrau)
title: The Parrot of India: Patiyali, the Seven Sultans, and the Grave at the Shaikh's Feet
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Kesh, the flight before the Mongols
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The family's origin at Kesh in Transoxiana and their passage through Balkh come from encyclopedic summary; no year is recorded for the migration, and the date shown is a placement inside the reign of Iltutmish, who died in 1236.
stops.campa: The family of Sayf al-Din Mahmud holds land at Kesh in Transoxiana, and the armies of Genghis Khan come west. They leave, pass through Balkh, and ride on to Delhi, where Sultan Shams al-Din Iltutmish is granting refuge and fiefs to the Turkish nobility running ahead of the Mongol road. Sayf al-Din is given the rank of amir and a garrison town called Patiyali on the Ganges plain. The poet later called the Parrot of India is not yet born. His father crosses two thousand miles of ruined country, and the birth happens at the far end of it, on the Ganges plain.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Aq Saray at Shahrisabz, later Timurid, standing on the Kesh the family left
sources: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Annemarie Schimmel, 'Amir Kosrow Dehlavi' (1989)

stops.name: Patiyali, the birth on the fief
stops.date_confidence: The year 1253 is standard across Iranica, Britannica and Wikipedia; no month or day is recorded and the date defaults to 01-01. Coordinate corrected: Patiyali stands at 27.717, 79.017, some 26 km south of the figure carried in the research pool, which fell on open country.
stops.campa: In a garrison town on his father's fief, near the Ganges in what is now Kasganj district, a son is born to the Turkish amir Sayf al-Din Mahmud and to an Indian mother, daughter of Imad ul-Mulk of the Delhi court. The house his father keeps speaks Persian and the town outside it speaks Hindavi, and the child takes both. He will spend fifty years writing Persian for sultans and Hindavi for everyone else, and will state the arrangement without apology: a Turk of Hindustan, answering in the language of the plain he was born on.
stops.quote: I am a Turk of Hindustan, I answer in Hindavi. I don't have Egyptian sugar to speak Arabic.
stops.quote_source: Amir Khusrau, quoted in Paul E. Losensky and Sunil Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (Penguin Classics, 2011), introduction
suggested_refs: The town of Patiyali on the Ganges in Kasganj district, birthplace and the only non-Delhi place he is claimed by

stops.name: Delhi, the father dead and the grandfather's house
stops.date_confidence: The father's death is dated 1260 and the grandfather's to 1273 by the standard biographies. Khusrow is seven at the loss, not the eight or nine repeated in secondary summaries, which is simple arithmetic on the 1253 birth. Imad ul-Mulk and Rawat Arz are one man, not two grandfathers. The age of 113 is household tradition. The pin is Qila Rai Pithora, the Mamluk city.
stops.campa: Sayf al-Din Mahmud dies when the boy is seven. Khusrow is taken into the Delhi household of his maternal grandfather Imad ul-Mulk, called Rawat Arz, an officer of the court with a Rajput establishment around him and, by his family's reckoning, a hundred and thirteen years behind him when he dies in 1273. The Turkish side of the family is now a dead man. The house that raises him is his mother's, Indian and old, and he will be inside a Persian court before he is twenty.
suggested_refs: The walls of Qila Rai Pithora at Mehrauli, the Delhi of Balban's generation

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the boy at the shaikh's door
stops.date_confidence: Khusrow's own preface to Wast ul-Hayat puts his finding of the shaikh at sixteen, which gives about 1269. The commonly cited date of formal discipleship is 1310. The two are not reconciled by any source reached and both are carried in this file as separate stops. Coordinate unified across lenses on the Nizamuddin Dargah at 28.5914, 77.2420.
stops.campa: Outside the walls, at Ghiyaspur, the Chishti shaikh Nizam ad-Din Auliya keeps a khanqah where food is given away faster than it comes in. Khusrow, by his own account in the preface to his second divan, is sixteen when he finds his guide there. The chain he attaches himself to runs back through Baba Farid and Qutb ad-Din Bakhtiar Kaki to Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer, and the robe that carries it passed through this same city in 1214. He will serve the courts of seven sultans across fifty years, and this one master throughout.
suggested_refs: The khanqah site at Ghiyaspur, now the Hazrat Nizamuddin Dargah complex
sources: Secondary accounts summarizing Khusrow's preface to Wast ul-Hayat
moinuddin_chishti.journey.json, stop 'Delhi, the khirqa to Baba Farid'

stops.name: Delhi, the gift of youth
stops.date_confidence: Dated 1271 by Wikipedia and the popular biographies, gathering verse of roughly his sixteenth to eighteenth years. Month and day not recorded.
stops.campa: He gathers the verse of his sixteenth to eighteenth years and closes it as a divan, Tuhfat us-Sighr, the Gift of Youth. It is the first of four collections he will close at intervals across his life: the Gift of Youth, the Middle of Life, the Prime of Perfection, and in old age the Remainder of the Pure. Delhi has Persian poets in numbers and several of them are good. None of them will produce work on this scale, and the second language of the streets they leave alone.
suggested_refs: Manuscript copies of Tuhfat us-Sighr, the first of the divans

segments.name: The Princes of the House of Balban

stops.name: Delhi, service with Malik Chhajju
stops.date_confidence: Reported by secondary biography only and dated 1272; no contemporary source reached names the appointment. The pin is central Delhi as a regional marker, since the household's seat is not specified and Chhajju's own fief lay at Kara.
stops.campa: His first place at a court is with Malik Chhajju, a nephew of Sultan Ghiyath al-Din Balban, and the verses written there are noticed above the level of the patron who commissioned them. A poet in this system is part of a prince's household equipment, kept for the praise he produces, and he moves when the household moves or falls. Khusrow will move again and again over fifty years, from nephew to son to grandson to usurper to the man who kills the usurper, and every move leaves a book behind it praising whoever holds Delhi that season.
suggested_refs: Persian court manuscripts of the Balban period, the milieu of the young panegyrist

stops.name: Delhi, into Bughra Khan's household
stops.date_confidence: 1276 for the entry into Bughra Khan's service and 1279 for the second divan are both carried by the standard chronology. Wikipedia places the divan's completion in Bengal, in the prince's service, which is impossible: Bughra Khan is not governor at Lakhnauti until 1281. This file keeps the date and drops the place.
stops.campa: Nasir al-Din Bughra Khan, a son of Balban, takes the poet into his service. The prince is companionable, fond of drink and of verse, and the connection outlasts his fortunes: Khusrow's first narrative poem, more than a decade off, will be built around a meeting between this prince and this prince's son. In the meantime there is the second divan to close, Wast ul-Hayat, the Middle of Life, finished in 1279, when its author is twenty-six and has already buried the two men who raised him.
suggested_refs: Manuscript copies of Wast ul-Hayat, the second divan

stops.name: Lakhnauti, the Bengal governorship
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and a corrected date. Bughra Khan's governorship of Lakhnauti runs 1281 to 1287 per Wikipedia and Banglapedia, and Balban does not return to Delhi until April 1282; the pool's date of 1279 for a visit to a governor not yet appointed is impossible. 1281 is the earliest year the journey could have happened. Pin is Gaur-Lakhnauti.
stops.campa: Balban marches on Bengal in 1281 to put down the rebellion of Tughril Tughan Khan, takes his son Bughra Khan with him, and when the rebel has been hunted down and killed installs the son at Lakhnauti as governor. The court that Khusrow's patron now keeps is six hundred miles from Delhi, on the edge of the delta, in a province that has revolted against every sultan who has held it. The poet's Bengal is dated by the tradition to 1279 and by the province's own history to no earlier than 1281.
suggested_refs: The brick ruins of Gaur-Lakhnauti on the Ganges, seat of the Bengal governors

stops.name: Multan, the gateway of India
stops.date_confidence: The Multan years are dated 1281 to 1285 by the standard chronology, which collides with the corrected earliest date for the Bengal journey; no source reached orders the two, and the month shown is a placement to keep them from occupying the same day. Multan Fort pin.
stops.campa: Khan Muhammad, Balban's eldest son and heir, governs Multan, the fortress the chroniclers call the gateway of India because every Mongol raid out of Khurasan arrives through it. Khusrow joins his household as court poet and serves five years inside a garrison that expects attack each season. The prince is the best patron the poet will ever have. In the same years the Chagatai armies are crossing the Indus in strength, and Delhi is holding this frontier with one prince and a wall.
suggested_refs: The fort and old city walls of Multan, frontier station of the Delhi Sultanate

stops.name: Multan, the prince rides out
stops.date_confidence: The date 9 March 1285 is attested. The engagement is conventionally the Battle of the Beas River in the Punjab, not a fight at Multan Fort, and Wikipedia gives the Chagatai commander as unknown; the name Timur Khan carried in the pool is unsupported. No coordinate for the battlefield was reached, so the pin is the city he rode out from. The captivity is disputed tradition: a few days per Mohammad Habib, two years at Balkh per Shibli Nomani, ransom rather than escape in other accounts.
stops.campa: On the ninth of March the Mongols come, and Khan Muhammad rides out to meet them. He is killed in the fighting, and the heir of the sultanate dies on a frontier his father sent him to hold. Khusrow is taken with the baggage and spends some period in Mongol hands that no two accounts measure the same way. What he brings back to Delhi is two elegies for a dead prince, and a line in which the weeping over him enlarges the geography of the Punjab by five rivers.
stops.quote: People shed so many tears in all directions that five other rivers have appeared in Multan.
stops.quote_source: Amir Khusrau, elegy for Khan Muhammad, in Losensky and Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (Penguin Classics, 2011), introduction, p. xix
suggested_refs: The Beas river in the Punjab, conventional site of the 1285 engagement

stops.name: Delhi, the court of Qaiqabad
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year by the standard chronology; month and day not recorded.
stops.campa: Balban dies and the throne goes to his grandson Muiz al-Din Qaiqabad, seventeen years old and interested in nothing that is not pleasure. Khusrow is taken into the court as poet. The old sultan's system of a hard frontier and a hard discipline goes slack inside a year, and everyone in Delhi can see what is coming for the house of Balban. Seeing it is not the poet's office. His office is the city, which he describes as the dome of Islam and the copy of paradise drawn out on an earthly page.
stops.quote: My home was the Dome of Islam. It was the qibla for kings of the seven climes. Delhi is the twin of pure paradise, a prototype of the heavenly throne on an earthly scroll.
stops.quote_source: Amir Khusrau, quoted in Losensky and Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (Penguin Classics, 2011), introduction, p. xvii
suggested_refs: The Qutb complex and the Mamluk city, the Delhi Khusrow calls the Dome of Islam
sources: Losensky and Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (2011)

stops.name: Northern Bihar, the father and the son
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction throughout. The only reachable source places the meeting of the two armies in Northern Bihar and names neither river nor year; this pin is a stand-in on the Ghaghara in Awadh with no attestation behind it, and it is the weakest coordinate in the file. The year is bracketed 1287 to 1289 by the composition of Qiran us-Sa'dain in 1289. Khusrow's presence as eyewitness is the tradition's claim.
stops.campa: Bughra Khan brings an army out of Bengal against his own son, and Qaiqabad brings the army of Delhi to meet it. The two hosts stand facing each other and no battle is fought. The father dismounts, the son comes down from the throne set up on the field, and the sultan of Delhi kisses his father's feet in front of both armies. Khusrow makes it the subject of his first masnavi, Qiran us-Sa'dain, the Conjunction of the Two Auspicious Planets, closed in 1289. His old patron and his new one meet in one poem.
suggested_refs: Manuscript copies of Qiran us-Sa'dain, the first of the masnavis

stops.name: Delhi, the title Amir and the keeper of the Qur'an
stops.date_confidence: The Khalji accession and Khusrow's promotion are attested to 1290; the third divan to 1294. Months and days not recorded. The quoted line on the two languages is undated within the corpus.
stops.campa: The house of Balban falls, Jalal al-Din Firuz Khalji takes Delhi, and the poet who praised the last three sultans is kept on and promoted. He is given the title Amir and the office of Mushaf-dar, keeper of the sultan's Qur'an, which is a place at the elbow of the throne. In 1294 he closes his third divan, Ghurrat ul-Kamal, the Prime of Perfection. He is forty-one, he has served four sultans, and he holds a plain opinion about which of his two languages is the immigrant.
stops.quote: Hindavi was the language from old times; when the Ghurids and Turks arrived in India, Persian began to be used.
stops.quote_source: Amir Khusrau, quoted in Losensky and Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (Penguin Classics, 2011), introduction, p. xxxvi
suggested_refs: Manuscript copies of Ghurrat ul-Kamal, the third divan

stops.name: Ranthambore, the siege that fails
stops.date_confidence: The campaign is dated 1290-91 and its failure attested: Jalal ud-Din besieged the fort briefly and did not take it. The masnavi is dated 1290 in one works table and 1291 in the chronology carried by the pool; the split is not resolved here. Whether Khusrow rode with the army or wrote from Delhi is not established. Coordinate corrected to the fort itself at 26.0203, 76.4550.
stops.campa: Jalal al-Din Khalji marches on the Chauhan fortress standing on its ridge above the Banas, sits down in front of it, and cannot take it. The army turns for Delhi with nothing. Khusrow makes a book of the campaign regardless, Miftah ul-Futuh, the Key to the Victories, and the title is doing the work the campaign did not. Four sultans in, he knows what a campaign poem is for, and the army that came back with nothing comes back into Persian verse with a fortress in the title.
suggested_refs: Ranthambore Fort on its ridge above the Banas, besieged twice in eleven years

stops.name: Kara-Manikpur, the governor on the Ganges
stops.date_confidence: Khusrow's presence at Kara is reconstruction and thinner than his attested Delhi years. Alauddin's governorship from about 1291 and the murder of Jalal al-Din on 19 July 1296 are attested. Coordinate corrected: Kara stands at 25.700, 81.350 in Kaushambi district, some 26 km from the pool's figure, which fell on the wrong side of the Yamuna.
stops.campa: Ali Gurshasp, nephew and son-in-law of the sultan, governs Kara on the Ganges and has been raiding south into Malwa and the Deccan for money the throne never sees. Some accounts put Khusrow in this provincial court in these years, attached to the household of the man about to become the most consequential sultan of the age. In July 1296 the nephew invites his uncle to a riverbank meeting at Kara, has him cut down on the bank, and rides for Delhi as Ala al-Din Khalji.
suggested_refs: The site of Kara on the Ganges in Kaushambi district, where Jalal al-Din was murdered

stops.name: Delhi, the killer keeps the poet
stops.date_confidence: Alauddin is proclaimed at Kara in July 1296 and reaches Delhi in the autumn; the standard chronology gives only the year for Khusrow's continuation at court, and the month shown is a placement.
stops.campa: The man who killed the last sultan takes the throne and keeps the last sultan's poet. Khusrow will serve Ala al-Din Khalji for twenty years, longer than he served anyone, and will write more under him than under all the others together: the quintet, the prose chronicle of the conquests, the romance of the sultan's son. Iranica sets the arrangement down without comment, that he was the favourite of Jalal al-Din and then the favourite of the man who murdered him.
suggested_refs: The Alai Darwaza and the unfinished Alai Minar, Alauddin's building at the Qutb

stops.name: Delhi, the answer to Nizami
stops.date_confidence: Dated 1298 by the standard chronology and by the Iranica entry on the Khamsa of Amir Khusrow; month and day not recorded.
stops.campa: A century after Nizami Ganjavi set five long poems in a fixed order and made them the shape Persian narrative verse must take, Khusrow writes five of his own against them, subject by subject, metre by metre. It is answer rather than imitation, and he says so himself at the end of the Hasht Bihisht, his reply to Nizami's Haft Paykar. The Khamsa-e-Khusrau is the work that carries his name out of India, into Herat and Tabriz and Istanbul, and into the hands of painters for three hundred years.
stops.quote: If honey is useful, vinegar too has its buyers.
stops.quote_source: Amir Khusrau, conclusion of the Hasht Bihisht, quoted in Losensky and Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (Penguin Classics, 2011), introduction
suggested_refs: Illustrated manuscripts of the Khamsa-e-Khusrau, the most copied of his works

stops.name: Delhi, the mother and the brother
stops.date_confidence: Dated 1300 by the standard chronology; no month, day, or circumstance is recorded. The pin is Delhi generally, since no residence is named.
stops.campa: His mother dies, and a brother with her. She is the Indian half of the house he was born into, daughter of the old man who took him in when his father died, and the reason an amir's son grew up with the language of the Ganges plain as a first tongue. Khusrow is forty-seven and at the height of what a court can give a poet. The elegies he wrote at Multan for a dead prince he now writes at home. Nothing else is recorded of either of them, not a name for the brother, not a cause for the deaths.
suggested_refs: The elegiac Persian ghazals of Khusrow's middle years

stops.name: Ranthambore, the fort taken
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1301; month and day not carried by the sources reached. Khusrow's presence with the royal camp is reported by summary sources and is not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: What Jalal al-Din could not do, the man who killed him does. Ala al-Din invests Ranthambore and keeps the army in front of it through a siege long enough to break the garrison, and the fort falls. Khusrow is with the king's camp and writes the campaign into the prose record he is assembling of this reign. The book he is building is not a masnavi. It is a chronicle in ornamented Persian prose, and it is the closest thing the age will leave to an eyewitness of what the Khalji armies did.
suggested_refs: Ranthambore Fort, taken by Alauddin in 1301 after Jalal al-Din's failure
sources: testbook.com, summary of the siege chronicles

stops.name: Chittorgarh, the eight months
stops.date_confidence: Siege dates 28 January to August 1303 attested; the fall is generally given as 26 August. Khusrow's presence is asserted by the standard chronology and by the eyewitness quality of the account.
stops.campa: The army sits down in front of Chittor on the twenty-eighth of January and stays until August. The fort on its plateau is the largest in India and the siege is the longest of the reign. When it falls Khusrow records it in Khazain ul-Futuh, and what he records is a siege: engines, mines, thirst, a surrender. The story of a Rajput queen called Padmini, a mirror, and a fire, attached to this siege two centuries later and now the best known thing about it, is in none of the early accounts, his own included.
suggested_refs: Chittorgarh Fort on its plateau, largest fort in India, besieged eight months in 1303

stops.name: Malwa, the western campaign
stops.date_confidence: Dated 1305 by summary sources. Whether Khusrow was in the field or worked from dispatches at Delhi is not established, and this stop is carried as reconstruction. The pin is the Mandu region as a marker for the province.
stops.campa: The Khalji armies go west into Malwa and take it. Khazain ul-Futuh has the conquest among the sultan's victories, in the same prose that handled Ranthambore and Chittor, and by now the shape of the book is fixed: a campaign is announced, the army is counted in astronomical figures, the fort submits, the chronicle moves on. The poet who spent his youth attached to individual princes now writes for a state with a standing army and a war on three fronts.
suggested_refs: The Malwa plateau and the fortress of Mandu, taken in the western campaigns
sources: researchdirections.org, summary of the Malwa campaign

stops.name: Devagiri, the Yadava capital
stops.date_confidence: Khusrow dates the invasion to March 1307 and narrates it after the siege of Siwana, which was fought August-September 1308; his own text is internally inconsistent. Kishori Saran Lal, following Barani, holds 1308 to be correct. The campaign was led by Malik Kafur, not by Alauddin in person. Both datings are left standing.
stops.campa: Malik Kafur, the eunuch general bought as a slave and risen to command everything, takes the army against Devagiri, the Yadava fortress on its rock in the Deccan, and brings back the tribute of the plateau. Khusrow dates the invasion to March and sets it after the siege of Siwana in the order of his book. Siwana falls in 1308. His own text will not let both stand, and the scholarship that came after him has been moving his months around ever since.
suggested_refs: The rock fortress of Devagiri, later Daulatabad, in the Deccan
sources: Kishori Saran Lal, History of the Khaljis

stops.name: Siwana, the hill fort
stops.date_confidence: Attested to August-September 1308, with Sitala Deva as defender. Coordinate corrected: Siwana lies at 25.633, 72.4167 in Balotra district, some 28 km south of the pool's figure.
stops.campa: In the hills of western Rajasthan the fort of Siwana holds out under Sitala Deva through August and into September before the Khalji army takes it. Khusrow puts it in the chronicle among the sultan's conquests. It is a small siege beside Chittor and it gets a small place in the book. It is also the fixed point on which the dating of the whole southern sequence turns, because the Devagiri campaign is narrated after it and cannot have happened before it.
suggested_refs: Siwana fort in Balotra district, Rajasthan, held by Sitala Deva

stops.name: Warangal, the Kakatiya tribute
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1310. Khusrow's personal presence with Kafur's army is disputed and this stop is carried as reconstruction; the account may have been compiled from dispatches at Delhi. The Koh-i-Noor in the indemnity is tradition.
stops.campa: Kafur takes the army eight hundred miles south to the Kakatiya capital and does not storm it. He invests it, accepts submission, and comes north with an indemnity that tradition says included the stone later called the Koh-i-Noor. Khazain ul-Futuh gives the fullest account of that march that exists in any language, in a Persian so ornamented that the geography has to be dug out of it. Whether he rode with the army or worked from dispatches at Delhi is not settled.
suggested_refs: Warangal Fort and the Kakatiya toranas, Telangana

stops.name: Dwarasamudra, the Hoysala capital
stops.date_confidence: Dated 1311. Khusrow's physical presence this far south is not confirmed; the eyewitness quality of the detail is an argument advanced by scholars, not a documented fact. Carried as reconstruction.
stops.campa: The army goes further, into the Hoysala country, and Dwarasamudra submits. Khusrow's account of this stretch describes ground covered in stones so sharp they tore the hooves from the cavalry's horses, which is the kind of detail a man does not get from a dispatch. It is an argument for his presence and it is not a proof of it. Delhi's writ has now been carried a thousand miles south of the Yamuna, and the man describing it was born on a fief near the Ganges.
suggested_refs: The Hoysaleswara temple at Halebidu, standing at the old Dwarasamudra
sources: Wikipedia, 'Malik Kafur's invasion of the Pandya kingdom'

stops.name: Madurai, the Pandya country
stops.date_confidence: The march date of 10 March 1311 is Khusrow's own. Khusrow's presence in the far south is reconstruction. Khazain ul-Futuh is completed about 1311-1312, since it narrates the Ma'bar campaign; the year 1296 given in some works tables is the year of Alauddin's accession, not of composition.
stops.campa: On the tenth of March the army leaves Dwarasamudra for the Pandya kingdom in the deep Tamil south, further than any Delhi force has gone. Khusrow records the date of the march and the hardship of it. Ma'bar is where the road ends: a country of temples and pearls at the tip of the peninsula, sacked rather than annexed, and the campaign that reaches it is the last great one of the reign. It is also the last event in the chronicle, which fixes when the chronicle was closed.
suggested_refs: The Pandya country of Ma'bar and the temple city of Madurai, southern limit of the Khalji raids
sources: Wikipedia, 'Malik Kafur's invasion of the Pandya kingdom'

stops.name: Siri, the chronicle closed
stops.date_confidence: Completion placed about 1311-1312 by the internal evidence of the Ma'bar campaign. The pin is Siri, the Khalji capital from 1303, rather than the Mamluk city used for the earlier Delhi stops; reusing one Delhi pin across three dynasties would flatten three successive capitals into one.
stops.campa: At Siri, the walled city Ala al-Din built in 1303 and made his seat, Khusrow closes Khazain ul-Futuh. It is prose and not verse, and it is the document on which everything later written about this reign depends. Its register is the register of conquest: temples are made to bow, forts lower their heads, the sea washes whatever the army has finished with. He will put the same wars into verse afterwards, in the Tarikh-i-Alai. The prose is where the campaigns are.
stops.quote: So the temple of Somnath was made to bow towards the Holy Mecca; and as the temple lowered its head and jumped into the sea, you may say that the building first said its prayers and then had a bath.
stops.quote_source: Amir Khusrau, Khazain ul-Futuh, trans. Mohammad Habib, cited in Jagdish Narayan Sarkar, The Art of War in Medieval India (1964), pp. 286-87
suggested_refs: The surviving wall stubs of Siri, Alauddin Khalji's capital from 1303
sources: Jagdish Narayan Sarkar, The Art of War in Medieval India (1964)

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the murid
stops.date_confidence: Two irreconcilable datings, both carried in this file. Secondary biographies give 1310 for formal initiation; Khusrow's own preface to Wast ul-Hayat puts his finding of the shaikh at sixteen, about 1269. Neither is dropped. Coordinate unified across lenses on the Nizamuddin Dargah at 28.5914, 77.2420.
stops.campa: The commonly cited date for Khusrow's formal discipleship under Nizam ad-Din Auliya is 1310, when he is fifty-seven and has been the first poet of three dynasties. His own preface says sixteen. Whatever the paperwork holds, the shaikh at Ghiyaspur takes nothing from any sultan and attends no court, and receives daily the courtier who serves them all. The shaikh will leave word that this one is to be buried beside him, because he cannot stand the thought of the separation.
suggested_refs: The baoli and khanqah precinct at Nizamuddin, Ghiyaspur, outside the Khalji walls

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the sama and what came of it
stops.date_confidence: No contemporary document fixes a date for this, and none names Khusrow as qawwali's originator; the attribution consolidates in later hagiography and is repeated as settled by modern accounts. The date shown is a placement inside his Ghiyaspur years, not an attested one.
stops.campa: At the khanqah the Chishtis hold sama, listening: singers perform before the shaikh and his circle, and the assembly is understood as worship. Tradition credits Khusrow with what that music became, Persian and Arabic modes joined to Indian ones and sung in both his languages at once, and calls it qawwali. Nothing written in the fourteenth century names him as its inventor. What is certain is that the repertoire sung at this shrine is full of his verse and has been for as long as anyone has been writing it down.
stops.quote: The king of the kingdoms of messengerdom, the tughra of the page of Majesty.
stops.quote_source: Amir Khusrau, na't in praise of the Prophet, quoted in Annemarie Schimmel, And Muhammad Is His Messenger (University of North Carolina Press, 1985), p. 205
suggested_refs: The qawwali platform at the Nizamuddin Dargah, where the repertoire is still sung nightly
sources: Darbar.org, 'Legendary Figures: Amir Khusrau and Gopal Nayak'
Schimmel, And Muhammad Is His Messenger (1985)

stops.name: Delhi, the instruments he did not invent
stops.date_confidence: Legend without a date; the year shown is a placement only. Wahid Mirza, his biographer, could confirm neither invention; instruments answering to the tritantri and saptantri predate him, and one line of argument assigns the sitar to a different and much later Amir Khusru of the eighteenth century. Sources contradict each other on whether the two men are the same. The tarana attribution is also traditional.
stops.campa: Tradition also gives him the sitar, cut down from a three-stringed tritantri and renamed seh-tar, and the tabla, split from a single drum into a pair. The musicologists have taken both away again. Instruments answering to those older names are older than he is, and one argument hands the sitar to a different Amir Khusru four centuries later. His own biographer Wahid Mirza could confirm neither. The tarana, the song made of syllables rather than words, is still his by common consent and by nothing firmer.
suggested_refs: Early sitars and tabla pairs in Indian instrument collections, all post-dating Khusrow by centuries
sources: Pragyata, 'Amir Khusrau's Contributions to Indian Music'

stops.name: Siri, the throne moves three times
stops.date_confidence: Alauddin's death on 4 January 1316 is attested, as are Malik Kafur's regency for Shihabuddin Omar, Kafur's murder, and Mubarak Shah's accession in April 1316. Summary chronologies that have Mubarak Shah succeed his father directly compress out an entire reign.
stops.campa: Ala al-Din Khalji dies on the fourth of January. Malik Kafur, the general who took the south for him, puts the dead sultan's child son Shihab al-Din Omar on the throne and rules as regent until the palace guard murder him some weeks later. Then Qutb al-Din Mubarak Shah, another son, has the child put aside and takes the throne himself in April. Three sultans in four months, and the general who conquered the south is dead in the middle of it. Khusrow is sixty-three, and he stays exactly where he is.
suggested_refs: Alauddin Khalji's tomb and madrasa at the Qutb complex, Mehrauli

stops.name: Siri, Duval Rani and Khizr Khan
stops.date_confidence: Dated 1315 in the pool's chronology and 1316 in the works table; the split is not resolved. The commission is Khizr Khan's own and not Alauddin's, and the tragic ending was added after Alauddin's death under Mubarak Shah, so the completed work postdates January 1316. The month shown is a placement.
stops.campa: Khizr Khan, Alauddin's son, asks Khusrow to write the story of his own love for Deval Devi, the Vaghela princess brought to Delhi out of Gujarat as a captive. The poet does it, a masnavi about people still alive, which is rare. Then the patron who asked for it is imprisoned, blinded and killed in the war over the succession, and Khusrow goes back into the poem and writes the death of the man who commissioned it into its ending. The romance and the elegy for its subject are bound in one volume.
suggested_refs: Mughal illustrated copies of Duval Rani wa Khizr Khan, a favourite subject of the ateliers
sources: Losensky and Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (2011)

stops.name: Siri, the Nine Skies
stops.date_confidence: Baqia-Naqia is dated 1317 and Nuh Sipihr 1318 by the works table. The quoted passage is verified against the full text of Elliot and Dowson Vol. III, p. 563; two versions of it circulating in secondary summaries are fabricated and reverse its sense.
stops.campa: In 1317 he closes another divan, Baqia-Naqia, the Remainder of the Pure. In 1318 he finishes Nuh Sipihr, the Nine Skies, a poem on Mubarak Shah's reign whose third sky turns away from the sultan altogether and argues India: its climate, its learning, its animals, its languages, and the superiority of the whole to anywhere the poet has heard of. He lists the tongues of the country region by region. He names Sanskrit and notes that the common people know nothing of it.
stops.quote: They have four books in that language, which they are constantly in the habit of repeating. Their name is Bed. They contain stories of their gods, but little advantage can be derived from their perusal.
stops.quote_source: Amir Khusrau, Nuh Sipihr, trans. in H. M. Elliot and John Dowson, The History of India as Told by Its Own Historians, Vol. III (1871), p. 563
suggested_refs: Mohammad Wahid Mirza's edition of Nuh Sipihr, and the third sky on the languages of India
sources: Elliot and Dowson, The History of India as Told by Its Own Historians, Vol. III (1871)

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the malfuz under his name
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, not attestation, and the pool's [A] tag is downgraded here. Dated 1319 and prose in genre per the works table, but the ascription is contested; Wikipedia itself warns that authenticity cannot be determined with confidence for works ascribed to Khusrow. No dedicated search of the scholarly dispute was possible within the research budget.
stops.campa: A book of the shaikh's table talk is set down under Khusrow's name: Afzal ul-Fawaid, prose, the sayings of Nizam ad-Din as a disciple heard them. The Chishti record of those conversations that scholarship trusts is a different book by a different disciple, Amir Hasan Sijzi's Fawa'id al-Fu'ad. Two poets sit in the same room hearing the same shaikh, and only one of them is now certain to have written down what was said. Books gather around a famous name. Which of the two poets set this one down is not settled by anything reached, and the ascription stands as an ascription.
suggested_refs: Amir Hasan Sijzi's Fawa'id al-Fu'ad, the securely attributed malfuzat of Nizam ad-Din Auliya

stops.name: Tughlaqabad, the fourth dynasty
stops.date_confidence: The assassination of Mubarak Shah and the dynastic change are attested to 1320. The Tughlaq Nama is dated 1320 in the works table and 'around 1321' by another lens of this research; 1320 is used and the disagreement is recorded. Tughlaqabad's construction begins in 1321. Coordinate corrected to 28.51194, 77.26083.
stops.campa: Mubarak Shah is murdered by his own favourite, who takes the throne as Nasir al-Din Khusrau Shah and holds it a few months, until Ghazi Malik, warden of the western marches, comes down on Delhi and destroys him. Ghazi Malik is crowned Ghiyath al-Din Tughlaq and begins at once a new capital of grey stone on the ridge southeast of the city, walls thirty feet thick. Amir Khusrow, sixty-seven, writes the Tughlaq Nama for the founder of the fourth dynasty he has served.
suggested_refs: The sloping grey walls of Tughlaqabad, begun 1321, and Ghiyath al-Din's tomb across the causeway

stops.name: Lakhnauti, away in the east
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The tradition has Khusrow away on a Tughlaq campaign in the east when his master died; the date shown is a placement inside that campaign, which the sources reached do not date. Pin is Gaur-Lakhnauti, the same as the 1281 stop.
stops.campa: Ghiyath al-Din Tughlaq marches east into Bengal, and the old poet goes with the court, forty-four years after he first came to this province in a dead prince's service. He is seventy-two. While he is there, on the third of April, Nizam ad-Din Auliya dies at Ghiyaspur, and the news has to cross the whole width of northern India to reach him. Fifty-six years of attendance at that khanqah, from the boy of sixteen to the old man in the sultan's baggage train, and the last journey of his life has him six hundred miles east on the day the shaikh dies.
suggested_refs: The Bengal road between Delhi and Lakhnauti, marched twice in one lifetime
sources: Losensky and Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (2011)

stops.name: Ghiyaspur, the doha at the grave
stops.date_confidence: The doha is printed by Losensky and Sharma as what Khusrow recited on hearing of the shaikh's death in 1325 while he was away in the east. The widely circulated variant ending 'rain bhayi chahun des' is an oral form and not the reading of that critical selection; it is a couplet, not a quatrain. The date is a placement, since no source gives the day of his return.
stops.campa: He comes back to Delhi and goes to the grave. What he says there is two lines of Hindavi and not a word of Persian, and it is built like a village song: the fair one sleeps on the bed with her hair fallen across her face, come away Khusrau, go home, evening has fallen over every country there is. He has written fifty years of Persian panegyric for seven sultans. The couplet is what he leaves at the grave, and the qawwals here are still singing it seven hundred years later.
stops.quote: gori sove sej par mukh par dare kes / chal Khusrau ghar apne sanjh bhai(n) sau des
stops.quote_source: Amir Khusrau, doha on the death of Nizam ad-Din Auliya, as printed in Losensky and Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (Penguin Classics, 2011)
suggested_refs: The doha as it is still sung by qawwals at the Nizamuddin Dargah
sources: Losensky and Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (2011)

stops.name: Nizamuddin, the grave at the shaikh's feet
stops.date_confidence: October 1325 per Wikipedia; Iranica gives 725 AH, that is 1325. The interval of about six months after the shaikh's death is the standard report and the cause of death given as grief is devotional tradition. Day not recorded.
stops.campa: Six months after his master, in October, Amir Khusrow dies in Delhi at seventy-two and is buried a few feet from him. Seven sultans of three dynasties employed him and every one of them lies somewhere else. He wrote Persian for the courts and Hindavi for the country and left behind four divans, a quintet answering Nizami, a prose chronicle that is the nearest thing to a record of the Deccan campaigns, and a body of song nobody can now reliably separate from what was later put under his name.
suggested_refs: The two graves at the Nizamuddin Dargah, shaikh and disciple, a few feet apart

stops.name: Delhi, the Moroccan arrives
stops.date_confidence: Ibn Battuta's arrival is dated 1334 in his own atlas file and the pin is inherited from it byte-identical. He and Khusrow never meet: the poet is nine years dead when the traveller rides in.
stops.campa: Nine years after the poet's death a traveller from Tangier rides into Delhi, is received by Muhammad bin Tughluq, given a house and villages for income, and made qadi of the capital. Ibn Battuta holds the post seven or eight years, judges through interpreters in a language he never learns, and writes the fullest outside description of this city that exists. The court Persian and the street Hindavi he moves between are the two Khusrow spent fifty years putting into verse, and Khusrow had already said what happens to a foreigner here.
stops.quote: If a Khurasani, Greek or Arab comes here, he will not face any problems, for the people will treat him kindly.
stops.quote_source: Amir Khusrau, quoted in Losensky and Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (Penguin Classics, 2011), introduction, p. xxxvi
suggested_refs: Ibn Battuta's Rihla, on the Delhi of Muhammad bin Tughluq
sources: ibn_battuta.journey.json, stop 'Delhi, qadi of the capital'
Losensky and Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (2011)

stops.name: Herat, the Khamsa illuminated
stops.date_confidence: The 1485 Khamsah miniature attributed to Bihzad at the Chester Beatty Library, Dublin, and further folios at the Metropolitan Museum of Art are attested; the wider manuscript tradition runs through the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. The Herat pin marks a workshop, not a place Khusrow ever went.
stops.campa: In the Timurid workshops at Herat the master Bihzad paints a manuscript of Khusrow's Khamsa, and the quintet becomes one of the standard vehicles of Persian and then Mughal miniature painting: Khusrau arriving at Shirin's palace, the eight paradises, the same scenes made again for three hundred years in Tabriz, Bukhara, Lahore and Agra. The folios are scattered now between Dublin and New York. No likeness made in the poet's lifetime survives, and every painted face of him is a later invention.
suggested_refs: The 1485 Bihzad Khamsah at the Chester Beatty Library, Dublin, and the Metropolitan Museum folios
sources: Barbara Brend, Perspectives on Persian Painting: Illustrations to Amir Khusrau's Khamsah (Routledge)
Metropolitan Museum of Art, collection record

stops.name: Nizamuddin Dargah, the marble of 1605
stops.date_confidence: The 1605 rebuilding under Jahangir by Khwaja Imad ud-Din Hassan is reported by site histories and is carried as reconstruction. Nothing of the 1325 grave marker survives. Pin unified on the dargah at 28.5914, 77.2420.
stops.campa: Under Jahangir, Khwaja Imad ud-Din Hassan builds the tomb that now stands over the grave: a marble dome, marble jali screens cut fine enough that the light comes through them like cloth, inside a red sandstone enclosure. Nothing of the 1325 marker is left underneath it. Two hundred and eighty years after the burial an empire is paying for the stonework, and the complex has become what it still is, a place where the urs of the shaikh and the urs of the poet are two feasts in one calendar.
suggested_refs: The marble tomb of Amir Khusrow, rebuilt 1605, inside the Hazrat Nizamuddin Dargah

stops.name: Calcutta, the texts edited
stops.date_confidence: The Nuh Sipihr edition is dated 1949 by the Internet Archive record digitized from the ASI Central Archaeological Library, not 1950 as carried in the pool. The Khazain edition, Calcutta 1953, and the 1975 Lahore translation are attested; the 1981 Jaipur translation could not be independently checked. The pin is Calcutta; Oxford, Lahore and Jaipur are named but not pinned.
stops.campa: Mohammad Wahid Mirza, who wrote the modern biography, edits the texts: Nuh Sipihr for Oxford University Press in 1949, Khazain ul-Futuh for the Asiatic Society at Calcutta in 1953. An English Khazain follows out of Lahore in 1975, for the committee marking seven hundred years since the poet's birth, and an English Nuh Sipihr out of Jaipur in 1981 under the title India as Seen by Amir Khusrau. Lahore and Calcutta are in different countries by then, and both of them are printing him.
suggested_refs: Wahid Mirza's editions of Nuh Sipihr (1949) and Khazain ul-Futuh (1953)
sources: Internet Archive, 'Nuh Sipihr Of Amir Khusrau: Mirza, Mohammad Wahid'

stops.name: Arab ki Sarai, Jahan-e-Khusrau
stops.date_confidence: Founded 2001 per Wikipedia, which is unambiguous; the hedge between 2000 and 2001 carried in the pool is unnecessary. A three-day festival held in February or March, annual with one gap in 2008.
stops.campa: Muzaffar Ali starts a three-day festival of Sufi music on the poet's death anniversary and holds the first of them in the caravanserai beside Humayun's tomb, half a mile from the grave. It runs every February or March, with one gap in 2008, and brings qawwals and Persian singers into a courtyard the Mughals built for pilgrims. The music played there is credited to a man no fourteenth-century document credits with it, in a city that has never once asked to see the document.
suggested_refs: Arab ki Sarai within the Humayun's Tomb complex, first venue of Jahan-e-Khusrau

stops.name: Delhi, the poems in English
stops.date_confidence: Published 2011 by Penguin Classics India; attested. It is the first broad English selection to print the Persian and the Hindavi together.
stops.campa: Paul Losensky and Sunil Sharma publish In the Bazaar of Love, the first wide English selection to put the Persian and the Hindavi between the same covers: ghazals, the doha at the grave, passages of Duval Rani and Khizr Khan. Their introduction prints the line about the Turk of Hindustan and the line about the parrot, and warns that when he claims he cannot manage Arabic he is posing. Seven centuries on, the two languages he refused to separate are in one book again.
stops.quote: I am a parrot of India if you ask me candidly. Ask me in Hindavi so that I can answer you correctly.
stops.quote_source: Amir Khusrau, quoted in Losensky and Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (Penguin Classics, 2011), introduction
suggested_refs: Losensky and Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love: The Selected Poetry of Amir Khusrau (Penguin Classics, 2011)
sources: Penguin Random House India, book page
Boston University, translation program profile of Sunil Sharma
